title: Decompose the Q4 jump
prompt: `df` has one row per non-cancelled order with `revenue`, `customer_id`, `coupon_code` and a `quarter` period. Build `q`, one row per quarter with `revenue` (sum), `orders` (count), `customers` (distinct customers) and `aov` (revenue ÷ orders). Then compute the Q3-to-Q4 2025 growth of revenue, orders and AOV as fractions (`revenue_growth`, `orders_growth`, `aov_growth`), the share of Q4 2025 revenue from `BLACKFRIDAY25` orders (`bf_share`), and the 2024 Q3-to-Q4 revenue growth (`growth_2024`). Round each of these five numbers to 3 decimals.
hints: `df.groupby("quarter").agg(revenue=("revenue", "sum"), orders=("order_id", "count"), customers=("customer_id", "nunique"))`, then add `aov` as a column.
Rows of `q` are labelled by period; `q.loc["2025Q4"] / q.loc["2025Q3"] - 1` gives every column's growth at once.
For the coupon share, filter Q4 2025 first, then divide the coupon orders' revenue by all Q4 revenue.
explanation: Dividing one row of `q` by another computes all the growth rates in one step, because the two rows share the same columns. Revenue +82.3% = orders +98.1% combined with AOV −8.0% (1.981 × 0.920 ≈ 1.823): the decomposition is exact, which is why it is such a powerful first move. Black Friday coupon orders were 8.4% of Q4 revenue, and the 2024 baseline shows Q4 was already about 73% above Q3 the year before. Together these numbers support the conclusion from the lesson: a normal seasonal peak on a much bigger business, driven by order volume.

checks.table: `q` has 8 quarters with revenue, orders, customers and aov
checks.q4-row: Q4 2025 shows 642 orders, 282 customers and an AOV of 228.70
checks.bf: Black Friday coupon orders are 8.4% of Q4 revenue
